name: Solar Panels and Photovoltaic Cells
what: This subtopic covers how photovoltaic (pv) cells convert sunlight into DC electricity, the energy transformations involved, the role of inverters in converting DC to AC, and how solar panels are connected in series and parallel circuits.
why: Solar panels are one of the most rapidly growing sources of electricity in Australia. Understanding how they work, and how to analyse their electrical behaviour, connects fundamental physics to real-world energy systems.

items.title: I can describe how a photovoltaic cell produces a DC potential difference
items.what: A photovoltaic (pv) cell is made from two types of doped silicon semiconductor joined at a pn junction. When sunlight falls on the cell, the photovoltaic effect causes electrons to move, creating a potential difference across the junction and producing DC electricity.
items.why: Understanding the basic mechanism of a pv cell explains why solar panels only ever produce DC voltage, which is essential for understanding why inverters are needed.
items.example: A typical household solar cell produces about 0.5 V DC. The doped silicon layers (n-type and p-type) create an internal electric field at the junction that drives electrons in one direction when light strikes the cell.

items.title: I can describe the energy transformation that occurs in a photovoltaic cell
items.what: In a pv cell, light energy (solar energy) is transformed into electrical energy. Some incoming energy is also converted into unwanted thermal energy. The efficiency of a modern commercial solar panel is up to approximately 25%.
items.why: Identifying energy transformations is a core physics skill and helps explain the limitations of solar technology, including why panels lose efficiency on hot days.
items.example: When 1000 W of sunlight falls on a 25%-efficient solar panel, approximately 250 W is converted to electrical energy and the remaining 750 W becomes heat.

items.title: I can explain the function of an inverter and why it is needed for household solar panels
items.what: An inverter is a device that converts the DC output of solar panels into AC electricity. It does this by rapidly switching the direction of the DC input. Australian households and the electricity grid use AC at 230 V, 50 Hz, so an inverter is necessary to make solar electricity usable.
items.why: Without an inverter, the DC from solar panels cannot directly power most household appliances or be fed back into the AC grid, making the inverter an essential component of any grid-connected solar system.
items.example: A string inverter might take 400 V DC from a series string of solar panels and convert it to 230 V AC at 50 Hz, which is then used by household appliances or exported to the grid.

items.title: I can compare the output of solar panels connected in series versus parallel
items.what: When solar panels are connected in series, their voltages add while the current stays the same. When connected in parallel, the voltage stays the same while their currents add. Power output is the same in both configurations for identical panels.
items.why: The choice of series or parallel connection determines the voltage and current delivered to an inverter or battery. Different inverters and applications require different voltage and current ranges.
items.example: Three panels each rated at 14.7 V and 27.2 A: in series, the total voltage is 44.1 V and current is 27.2 A (power = 1199 W). In parallel, voltage is 14.7 V and current is 81.6 A (power = 1199 W).

items.title: I can calculate voltage, current and power for solar panels in series and parallel combinations
items.what: Using the rules for series and parallel circuits: in series, voltages add and current is shared; in parallel, voltage is shared and currents add. Power for any configuration is found using P = VI.
items.why: These calculations are required both in exam contexts and in real solar installation design, where engineers must match panel configurations to inverter specifications.
items.example: Two panels (400 W, 14.7 V, 27.2 A) in series: V_total = 29.4 V, I_total = 27.2 A, P_total = 29.4 × 27.2 = 799.5 W ≈ 800 W.
